correctness.rationale: A direct generating-function extraction proves the target is [q]H_{r-1}. The integer binomial basis coefficients have exact first two leading forms; an induction proves a_{k,j} is divisible by m^(k+j-1). The only possible second low-degree obstruction is alpha_3(1)=binom(m,3), divisible by m when gcd(m,6)=1, yielding a scalar congruence modulo m^(k+2) for a_{k+1,1}. The unit is invertible modulo m, proving sharpness. The attached standalone checker reproduced 29 units, four direct counts, and 24 polynomial identities. Finite checks are not the proof.

originality.rationale: Published sources prove divisibility and describe extraction machinery, but the precise first nonzero m-adic digit and its nonvanishing for arbitrary depths are a separate consequence requiring an extra weighted coefficient induction. No indexed covering assertion was found; older and unindexed equivalents remain residual risks.
residual_risks: An unindexed statement or a previously unnoticed exact specialization of older work could express the same unit; this is not ruled out by search.
The older 1970 Rødseth original was not independently read in full, but its relevant congruence is restated explicitly in the inspected 2001 paper.

General higher-power computation methods could in principle be specialized to derive this identity; the novelty claim is the explicit uniform congruence and proof, not its logical independence from all published algorithms.

value.rationale: Sharpens a classical m-ary partition congruence for an infinite natural family: exact nonzero leading m-adic digit at every depth, exact prime-adic valuations for all p>=5, and a multiplicative-order profile for normalized units. The unit is motivated by the precision gap between known lower divisibility and exact valuation, not an arbitrary finite slice. The special restriction to gcd(m,6)=1 is motivated by a genuine binomial obstruction at 3.
